title: Polymath Robotics Blog | ROS2 Graph Monitor: A Continuous Snapshot of Your Robot’s State
summary: Meet our open-source ROS2 Graph Monitor with a Foxglove extension -- giving engineers a continuous, queryable snapshot of their robot’s system state to simplify debugging and analysis.
body_text: For years, ROS 2 users have struggled to get a clear and complete snapshot of their system state at a moment in time. Today, we're excited to announce our open-source work on ROS2 Graph Monitor in conjunction with a Foxglove extension to help solve that problem: The problem we're solving ROS2 is made up of nodes that connect to each other through topics, services, and actions. When something goes wrong, being able to see the exact connections at the moment of failure is critical. But the existing options to do this introspection have always been clunky. You might run a script on the robot to spit out a static image of the graph, but that's not something you can easily query later or pair with a bag recording to make the debugging process easier. And due to the distributed nature of a ROS 2 application, this is not easy to do instantaneously, it is better solved by a long-running observer of the system. If a graph-related issue happened in the field two weeks ago, you'd be out of luck. How ROS Graph Monitor came to be On the Polymath team, we've wanted the capability to assess the health of the ROS2 graph for a long time. Emerson Knapp released an initial version with his ROSCon 2024 talk on the subject (side note: that was how the Polymath team first connected with him!). Shortly after, we brought that work into the Polymath stack. While we ran the rosgraph monitor continuously, it wasn’t until our engineer Dhruv Tyagi decided to build a ROS graph visualizer in Foxglove Studio that things started to click: we could pair Dhruv’s visualizer with a publisher that continuously outputs the graph structure. That way, you could record the graph state alongside other telemetry and inspect it any time. How it works The system we’re discussing is made of two independent components. One component, the graph monitor, observes and publishes the ROS graph - every node, topic, parameter and connection - at a set interval and whenever something changes. With this information available, you can use the Foxglove panel to explore it visually. Now, if you have a bag file from that weird day in the field, you can jump back in time and see exactly what the system looked like. You can spot which topics were active, how often they were publishing, and whether something drifted from its normal state. Why it matters Say your costmap generation has degraded. You suspect your LiDAR is publishing at a reduced rate. With ROS Graph Monitor, you can pull up a snapshot from before and during the problem, see the drop from 20Hz to a much lower rate, and confirm the basic root cause without trawling through individual messages. It's almost like running a blood panel for your robot. You are not looking at every individual reading, just the high-level state (and variances from expected values) that tells you where to focus. Open source and ready to use The ROS Graph Monitor is now released into ROS 2 distributions, and the Foxglove extension is now open source. You can use them in your application today, and soon the extension will be available on the Foxglove public registry. What's next There is an active backlog for both of these tools. Visualizing topic frequencies is high on the list, so you could glance at the graph and see which areas are “hot” and which are “cold.” There is also a lot of room for improvement in the rendering of the ROS graph in the panel. These kinds of tools don't directly make a robot more reliable, but they make engineers far more effective. The faster you can see what is going on, the faster you can fix it. ‍

title: B2B Payments in Africa: The Complete Guide to Business Payments, Challenges, and Solutions in 2026
summary: Discover everything about B2B payments in Africa. Learn about, challenges, providers, and how African businesses can optimize cross-border...
body_text: What Are B2B Payments? Business-to-business (B2B) payments are financial transactions between businesses for goods or services. Unlike business-to-consumer (B2C) payments, where a customer buys a product and pays immediately, B2B payments involve more complexity, higher transaction values, extended payment terms, and multiple approval layers. Key Characteristics of B2B Payments Higher Transaction Values : B2B payments typically involve significantly larger amounts than consumer transactions. While a B2C payment might be $50 for a retail purchase, B2B transactions can range from thousands to millions of dollars for supplier invoices, bulk orders, or service contracts. Extended Payment Terms : Unlike instant consumer payments, B2B transactions often operate on credit terms such as Net 30, Net 60, or Net 90 (payment due in 30, 60, or 90 days). These terms help businesses manage cash flow but create additional complexity in payment processing and reconciliation. Complex Approval Workflows : B2B payments require multiple internal stakeholders to review and approve transactions. A single payment might need sign-off from procurement, finance, legal, and executive teams before processing. Rich Transaction Data : B2B payments carry extensive metadata including purchase order numbers, invoice details, tax information, cost center allocations, and compliance documentation. This data is essential for accounting reconciliation and audit trails. Recurring and One-Time Transactions : B2B payments can be recurring (monthly software subscriptions, regular supplier payments) or one-time (project-based services, equipment purchases), requiring flexible payment systems. The African B2B Payments Landscape: A $200+ Billion Opportunity Africa’s B2B payments market represents one of the continent’s most significant untapped opportunities, valued at over $200 billion annually and growing rapidly. To understand this opportunity, we need to examine the unique characteristics of Africa’s business payment ecosystem. Market Size and Growth Trajectory The African B2B payments market is experiencing unprecedented growth driven by several converging factors: SME Dominance : Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) represent approximately 90% of businesses across Africa and contribute over 50% of employment. These businesses form the backbone of intra-African trade and represent the primary drivers of B2B payment volume. Mobile Money Revolution : Africa leads the world in mobile money adoption, with mobile money transaction values reaching $1.4 trillion in 2023 , up 39% from $495 billion in 2020. This infrastructure provides the foundation for digital B2B payment transformation. Cross-Border Trade Growth : The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which launched in 2021, creates a single market of 1.3 billion people with a combined GDP of $3.4 trillion. This integration is accelerating intra-African trade and creating massive demand for efficient cross-border B2B payment solutions. Digital Payment Growth : Digital payment systems in Africa have grown by 37% in transaction volume over the past five years, signaling a fundamental shift from cash-based to digital business transactions. Regional Payment Infrastructure Variations Africa’s 54 countries present a highly fragmented payment landscape with significant regional variations: West Africa : Dominated by Nigeria’s massive economy, West Africa combines traditional banking infrastructure with innovative mobile money solutions. Countries like Ghana, Côte d’Ivoire, and Senegal are rapidly digitalizing their payment systems. East Africa : Led by Kenya’s M-Pesa revolution, East Africa represents the most advanced mobile money ecosystem globally. Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and Rwanda have built robust digital payment infrastructure enabling seamless business transactions. Southern Africa : South Africa maintains the most developed traditional banking infrastructure on the continent, with sophisticated electronic payment systems. However, other Southern African countries like Zambia and Zimbabwe are leapfrogging to mobile-first solutions. North Africa : Countries like Egypt and Morocco have well-established banking systems but face unique regulatory environments. The region is gradually opening to innovative fintech solutions. The Informal Economy Challenge and Opportunity One defining characteristic of African B2B payments is the significant role of informal business transactions. An estimated 85-90% of businesses in Sub-Saharan Africa operate informally or semi-formally, presenting both challenges and opportunities: Cash Dependency : Many businesses still rely heavily on cash transactions due to limited access to formal financial services, creating inefficiencies and security risks. Formalization Through Payments : Digital B2B payment solutions serve as catalysts for business formalization. When informal businesses gain access to digital payment infrastructure, they can build transaction histories, access credit, and integrate into formal supply chains. Financial Inclusion Gap : Over 800 million Africans still lack access to formal financial services. B2B payment providers that can serve informal and semi-formal businesses unlock massive market potential while driving financial inclusion. Why B2B Payments Matter for African Businesses Efficient B2B payment systems are not merely operational conveniences—they are fundamental enablers of business growth, economic development, and continental integration. Here’s why B2B payments matter critically for African businesses: Expense Management Optimization Expense management represents one of the most significant challenges for African businesses, particularly SMEs. Traditional payment methods like checks and manual bank transfers can take 3-5 days to settle, tying up working capital that businesses need for operations. Faster Settlement Times : Modern B2B payment solutions offer same-day or next-day settlement, dramatically improving cash flow. When a Kenyan exporter can receive payment from a Nigerian buyer within 24 hours instead of a week, they can reinvest those funds immediately into inventory or operations. Predictable Payment Timing : Digital payment systems provide visibility into when funds will arrive, enabling better financial planning and reducing the need for expensive short-term financing. Reduced Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) : Businesses using efficient B2B payment solutions typically see their DSO decrease by 15-30%, meaning they collect payments faster and maintain healthier cash positions. Enabling Cross-Border Trade Intra-African trade has historically been constrained by payment friction. Before the rise of modern payment infrastructure, sending money between African countries was often more expensive and slower than sending money from Africa to Europe or North America. Reduced Transaction Costs : Traditional cross-border payments in Africa could cost 7-12% in fees. Modern B2B payment platforms have reduced this to 1-3%, making cross-border payments economically viable for smaller businesses. Currency Conversion Efficiency : Businesses can now accept payments in customers’ local currencies and receive settlement in their preferred currency, eliminating the complexity of managing multiple currency accounts. AfCFTA Facilitation : Efficient B2B payments are essential infrastructure for realizing the African Continental Free Trade Area’s potential. A Nigerian retailer sourcing products from South Africa needs seamless payment rails to make that trade relationship viable. Building Business Credibility and Relationships In Africa’s relationship-driven business culture, reliable payment execution is crucial for building trust and long-term partnerships. Vendor Relationship Management : Businesses that pay suppliers reliably and on-time build stronger relationships, often securing better payment terms, priority service, and preferential pricing. Customer Trust : For businesses receiving payments, offering multiple convenient payment options and processing payments securely builds customer confidence and encourages repeat business. Access to Financing : Businesses with documented digital payment histories can leverage transaction data to access working capital loans, trade finance, and other financial services previously unavailable to them. Operational Efficiency and Cost Reduction Manual payment processes consume significant staff time and resources while introducing error risks. Reduced Administrative Burden : Automating payment processes can reduce finance team workload by 40-60%, allowing staff to focus on strategic activities rather than payment processing and reconciliation. Lower Error Rates : Manual payment entry and reconciliation introduces errors costing businesses time and money. Digital B2B payment systems with automated reconciliation reduce error rates by over 80%. Audit Trail and Compliance : Digital payment systems automatically generate comprehensive audit trails, simplifying compliance with tax regulations, financial reporting requirements, and audit processes Types of B2B Payment Methods in Africa African businesses can choose from various B2B payment methods, each with distinct advantages, limitations, and use cases. Understanding these options enables businesses to optimize their payment strategies. 1. Bank Transfers and Wire Payments Bank transfers remain the most common B2B payment method across Africa, particularly for larger transactions. How They Work : Direct account-to-account transfers through the banking system, including local transfers (within the same country) and international wire transfers (cross-border). Advantages in African Context : Widely accepted across all business sizes and sectors Suitable for large transaction values Established regulatory framework Creating formal transaction records for compliance and financing Limitations : Slow settlement times (2-5 business days for local, 3-7 days for international) High costs for cross-border transactions (5-12% in fees) Limited transparency in payment status Requires banking infrastructure access Manual reconciliation processes Best Use Cases : Large B2B transactions, supplier payments with extended terms, formal contracts with established businesses. 2. Mobile Money Payments Mobile money represents Africa’s most significant payment innovation, with over 500 million registered mobile money accounts across the continent. How It Works : Digital wallet-based payments through mobile phones, originally designed for person-to-person transfers but increasingly adapted for business payments. Advantages in African Context : Accessible without traditional bank accounts Fast transaction processing (often instant) Wide reach, especially in East and West Africa Lower costs than traditional banking for smaller transactions Familiar to most African business owners Limitations : Transaction limits (typically $500-$5,000 maximum) Limited cross-border functionality Less suitable for very large B2B transactions Variable liquidity across different networks Reconciliation challenges with multiple providers Best Use Cases : SME-to-SME payments, last-mile supplier payments, informal and semi-formal business transactions, markets with limited banking infrastructure. 3. Credit and Debit Card Payments Card payments are gaining adoption in African B2B transactions, particularly for online purchases and recurring payments. How They Work : Payments processed through card networks (Visa, Mastercard, Verve) either through physical terminals or online payment gateways. Advantages in African Context : Instant payment confirmation Convenient for online and recurring transactions Fraud protection mechanisms Integration with accounting software Suitable for international suppliers Limitations : Processing fees (2.5-4% typically) Not universally accepted by B2B suppliers Security concerns in some markets Card limits may restrict large transactions Requires payment terminal or online gateway infrastructure Best Use Cases : Software subscriptions, online B2B marketplaces, digital services, international supplier payments, recurring service fees. 4. Virtual Bank Accounts Virtual bank accounts represent an emerging solution gaining traction across African B2B payments. How They Work : Businesses receive unique virtual account numbers for each customer or payment purpose, simplifying reconciliation while payments settle into a single master account. Advantages in African Context : Automated reconciliation (each customer has unique account) Professional payment experience Reduces manual payment matching Suitable for recurring payments Works within existing banking infrastructure Limitations : Requires partnership with payment provider offering virtual accounts Not yet universally available across all African countries May have setup costs or ongoing fees Customers must have banking access Best Use Cases : SaaS businesses, subscription services, marketplace platforms, businesses with high payment volumes requiring automated reconciliation. 5. Payment Links and Digital Invoices Payment links are increasingly popular for B2B transactions, especially among digitally savvy businesses. How They Work : Businesses send payment links via email, SMS, or messaging apps. Customers click the link and pay using their preferred method (card, mobile money, bank transfer). Advantages in African Context : No website required to accept digital payments Multiple payment methods in one link Fast payment collection Reduces payment friction Trackable payment status Limitations : Requires customers to have digital payment access Processing fees apply (varies by payment method) Less formal than traditional invoicing May require customer education Best Use Cases : Service businesses, freelancers and agencies, businesses without e-commerce infrastructure, invoice payments, deposit collection. 6. Checks (Declining Usage) While still used in some African markets, checks are rapidly declining as a B2B payment method. Advantages : Familiar to traditional businesses Physical record of payment Accepted by older business systems Limitations : Slow processing (5-10 business days) Security risks (fraud, theft, loss) High bank processing fees Increasingly phased out by banks Manual reconciliation required Current Status : Many African banks are phasing out check services entirely. Businesses still using checks should transition to digital alternatives. 7. Cash (High Risk, Declining) Despite modernization, cash remains prevalent in African B2B transactions, particularly in informal sectors and last-mile supply chains. Why It Persists : Universal acceptance without infrastructure requirements Immediate settlement Privacy and simplicity Habit and cultural factors Limited access to formal payment systems Significant Risks : Theft and security concerns No transaction records for compliance or financing Counting and transport costs Fraud and counterfeit currency Prevents business formalization Future Trajectory : Cash usage in B2B payments is declining as digital infrastructure expands, but will remain relevant in certain sectors for the near term Challenges Facing B2B Payments in Africa While Africa’s B2B payment landscape is evolving rapidly, businesses still face significant challenges that create friction, increase costs, and limit growth potential. 1. Fragmented Payment Infrastructure Africa’s 54 countries operate largely independent payment systems with limited interoperability, creating major obstacles for businesses operating across borders. Multiple Integrations Required : A business serving customers in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa may need separate integrations with 4-10 different payment providers, each with different APIs, documentation, and requirements. Regulatory Complexity : Each country has unique central bank regulations, licensing requirements, KYC rules, and compliance standards. Navigating this regulatory maze requires significant resources. Currency Management : Managing 42+ different currencies across the continent, each with different exchange rates, volatility profiles, and conversion costs, adds operational complexity. Limited Cross-Border Rails : Unlike Europe’s SEPA system or North America’s ACH network, Africa lacks unified payment rails enabling seamless cross-border transactions at reasonable costs. 2. High Transaction Costs The cost of B2B payments in Africa remains significantly higher than in developed markets, particularly for cross-border transactions. Cross-Border Payment Costs : International payments within Africa can cost 7-12% in fees, compared to 1-2% in developed markets. A Nigerian business paying a Kenyan supplier $10,000 might pay $800-$1,200 in fees alone. Multiple Fee Layers : Businesses face layered costs including bank fees, correspondent bank fees, foreign exchange markups, intermediary charges, and receiving fees—often with limited transparency. Currency Conversion Spreads : Foreign exchange spreads in African corridors can range from 3-8%, significantly higher than the 0.5-1.5% typical in major currency pairs. Impact on Small Transactions : High fixed fees make smaller B2B transactions economically unviable. A $500 payment with $50 in fees represents a 10% cost, discouraging trade. 3. Speed and Transparency Challenges Traditional B2B payments in Africa suffer from slow processing times and poor visibility, creating cash flow challenges and uncertainty. Settlement Delays : Domestic bank transfers can take 2-5 business days, while cross-border payments often require 3-7 business days or longer, tying up working capital. Limited Payment Tracking : Traditional payment methods offer minimal visibility into payment status. Businesses often don’t know if payments are processing, delayed, or failed until days after initiation. Cut-Off Times and Banking Hours : Payments initiated after banking cut-off times (often 2-3 PM) won’t process until the next business day. Weekend and holiday delays further extend settlement times. Time Zone Complications : Cross-border payments crossing multiple time zones face additional delays as banks in different countries process transactions sequentially. 4. Foreign Exchange Volatility and Risk Currency volatility in African markets creates significant risk for B2B transactions, particularly those with deferred payment terms. Exchange Rate Fluctuations : Some African currencies experience 5-20% annual volatility against major currencies. A 30-day payment term can expose businesses to significant exchange rate risk. Limited Hedging Options : Small and medium businesses typically lack access to forex hedging instruments available to large corporations, leaving them exposed to currency risk. Pricing Complexity : Businesses must decide whether to price in local currency (accepting exchange risk) or foreign currency (potentially reducing competitiveness and shifting risk to customers). 5. Limited Access to Payment Infrastructure Many African businesses, particularly SMEs and those in rural areas, face barriers accessing modern payment infrastructure. Banking Access Gaps : Despite mobile money growth, many businesses still lack access to commercial bank accounts, particularly in rural areas and among informal businesses. Technology Infrastructure : Unreliable internet connectivity and power supply in some regions limit ability to use digital payment platforms. Digital Literacy : Business owners and staff may lack familiarity with digital payment tools, creating adoption barriers even when infrastructure exists. Capital Requirements : Some payment solutions require upfront investments in hardware (POS terminals) or software that small businesses struggle to afford. 6. Reconciliation and Accounting Complexity Manual payment reconciliation consumes significant time and resources for African businesses while introducing error risks. Multiple Payment Sources : Businesses receiving payments through bank transfers, mobile money, cards, and cash must manually reconcile transactions from different sources with different data formats. Missing or Incomplete Payment Information : Customers often fail to include invoice references or payment details, making it difficult to match payments to invoices. Manual Data Entry : Finance teams spend hours manually entering payment data into accounting systems and matching payments to receivables. Error and Dispute Resolution : Reconciliation errors create disputes with suppliers and customers, requiring additional time to investigate and resolve. 7. Security and Fraud Concerns As African B2B payments digitalize, security and fraud present growing concerns for businesses. Business Email Compromise (BEC) : Fraudsters impersonate suppliers or executives via email to redirect payments to fraudulent accounts. BEC scams targeting businesses increased 200% in some African markets during 2023-2024. Payment Fraud : Invoice fraud, account takeover, and identity theft pose significant risks, particularly as businesses adopt digital payment methods without adequate security measures. Limited Fraud Protection : Many small businesses lack sophisticated fraud detection tools and insurance coverage available to larger enterprises. Cybersecurity Vulnerabilities : Businesses with limited IT resources may have weak cybersecurity practices, making them vulnerable to payment-related attacks. Digital Transformation of B2B Payments in Africa Africa is experiencing a profound digital transformation in B2B payments, driven by technology innovation, changing expectations, and the need for greater efficiency. This transformation mirrors the “consumerization” of B2B payments seen globally but with uniquely African characteristics. From Cash to Digital: The Paradigm Shift African businesses are rapidly moving from cash-based and manual processes toward digital-first payment approaches: Mobile-First Infrastructure : Unlike developed markets that evolved from cash to checks to cards to digital, many African businesses are leapfrogging directly from cash to mobile and digital payment solutions. API-Driven Integration : Modern payment platforms offer API-first approaches enabling businesses to integrate payments directly into their operational systems, automating previously manual processes. Real-Time Expectations : Business owners who experience instant mobile money transfers in their personal lives increasingly expect similar speed in their business transactions. Data-Driven Decision Making : Digital payment systems generate rich transaction data enabling businesses to analyze payment patterns, optimize cash flow, and make data-driven decisions. Key Digital Payment Innovations in African B2B Space Several technological innovations are reshaping African B2B payments: Unified Payment APIs : Platforms like Duplo enable businesses to access multiple payment methods (bank transfers, virtual accounts) across multiple countries through a single API integration, dramatically reducing complexity. Virtual Card Issuing : Businesses can issue virtual debit cards for employees and suppliers, enabling controlled spending with real-time visibility and spending limits. Automated Reconciliation : AI-powered reconciliation systems automatically match incoming payments to invoices using pattern recognition and machine learning, reducing manual work by 80%+. Real-Time Settlement : Some payment providers now offer instant or same-day settlement in local currencies, dramatically improving cash flow compared to traditional T+3 or T+5 settlement cycles. Multi-Currency Wallets : Businesses can hold and manage balances in multiple African currencies, making strategic decisions about when to convert currencies based on exchange rates. Blockchain and Stablecoins : Emerging use of blockchain technology and stablecoins for cross-border B2B payments offers potential for faster, cheaper international transactions, though regulatory frameworks remain evolving. Benefits of Digital B2B Payment Transformation African businesses adopting digital B2B payment solutions realize multiple benefits: Cost Reduction : Digital payments reduce transaction costs by 30-60% compared to traditional methods while eliminating cash handling expenses. Time Savings : Automation reduces payment processing time from hours to minutes and eliminates manual reconciliation work, allowing finance teams to focus on strategic activities. Improved Cash Flow : Faster settlement times and better cash flow visibility enable businesses to operate with less working capital and reduce need for expensive short-term financing. Enhanced Security : Digital payment systems with encryption, multi-factor authentication, and fraud monitoring provide significantly better security than cash or checks. Scalability : Digital infrastructure enables businesses to scale payment operations without proportionally increasing staff or costs. Access to Financing : Transaction data from digital payment systems enables businesses to access working capital loans, invoice financing, and other financial services. Customer Experience : Offering customers multiple convenient payment options improves satisfaction and conversion rates Top B2B Payment Solutions in Africa Africa’s B2B payment ecosystem includes several established players and innovative newcomers. Understanding the landscape helps businesses choose solutions aligned with their needs. 1. Duplo Overview : Founded in 2021, Duplo is a Nigerian-based fintech simplifying B2B payments in Africa . The company provides businesses with an integrated platform to automate payables, receivables, and expense management while enabling fast, affordable cross-border payments across multiple currencies. Duplo’s mission is to help African businesses eliminate manual finance processes, improve visibility, and gain real-time control over how money moves within and beyond their organizations. Geographic Coverage: Currently operational in Nigeria, with expanding cross-border payment coverage across key African markets including Ghana, Kenya, Côte d’Ivoire, and South Africa, and support for international transactions in USD, GBP, EUR, CAD, and other major currencies. Core Products: Payments: Manage local and international payouts and collections from a single dashboard. Payments can be made from a funded wallet or directly from bank accounts linked to the platform. Expense & Spend Management: Automate approval workflows, track team expenses in real time, and set departmental budgets for greater financial control. Reconciliation & Reporting: Gain full visibility into cash flow with automated reconciliations, audit-ready reports, and compliance monitoring. Vendor & Tax Management: Pay vendors faster, automatically calculate taxes, and maintain accurate financial records for regulatory compliance. Virtual Accounts: Generate dedicated virtual accounts for departments, vendors, and customers to simplify collections and tracking. Key Differentiators: All-in-One B2B Payment Platform: Combines local and cross-border payments, expense management, and reporting in one system. Speed & Affordability: Enables fast, low-cost transfers across Africa and international corridors. Automated Workflows: Reduces manual processing through smart approval flows and real-time reporting Finance Transparency: Real-time dashboards offer visibility into spending, approvals, and tax settlements. Compliance & Security: Built with enterprise-grade data protection and regulatory compliance frameworks. Best For: Enterprises and mid-sized businesses operating across multiple African markets that need a reliable platform for B2B payments, cross-border transactions, expense automation, and financial reconciliation. 2. Interswitch Overview : Founded in 2002 as a consortium of Nigerian banks and strategic partners, Interswitch pioneered Nigeria’s electronic payment infrastructure when the country had few ATMs and virtually no POS systems. Geographic Coverage : Primarily Nigeria with expanding African presence. Core Strengths : Deep Nigerian Market Penetration : Processes a substantial portion of Nigeria’s electronic payment volume Verve Card Scheme : Over 70 million Africans hold Verve cards, providing domestic card payment capabilities Quickteller Platform : Connects 8,000+ billers enabling businesses to accept payments from extensive digital and physical touchpoints Institutional Relationships : Decades-long partnerships with Nigerian banks, government entities, and large corporations Best For : Businesses operating primarily in Nigeria, enterprises requiring deep banking system integration, businesses needing extensive biller network access, and organizations prioritizing established infrastructure over cutting-edge developer experience. 3. Flutterwave Overview : Founded in 2016 by Iyinoluwa Aboyeji and Gbenga Agboola, Flutterwave emerged with a vision to enable African businesses to transact seamlessly with the global economy. The company pioneered a developer-first approach to African payments. Geographic Coverage : Operations across 34+ African countries with strong presence in Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana, and South Africa. Core Strengths : Global Connectivity : Extensive international payment partnerships enabling African businesses to accept payments globally Enterprise Client Base : Processes payments for Uber, Facebook (Meta), Booking.com, MTN, and other global enterprises Comprehensive Product Suite : Cards, mobile money, bank transfers, payment links, virtual cards, and remittances Developer-Focused Platform : Clean APIs, extensive documentation, and developer support Best For : Businesses with global payment needs, enterprises requiring reliability at scale, digital platforms serving international customers, and businesses prioritizing comprehensive payment options. 4. Paystack (A Stripe Company) Overview : Founded in 2016, Paystack revolutionized Nigerian online payments by making integration remarkably simple for developers and businesses. Acquired by Stripe for over $200 million in 2020, Paystack brought Silicon Valley’s payment excellence to Africa. Geographic Coverage : Primarily Nigeria, Ghana, and South Africa with expansion plans. Core Strengths : Developer Experience : Industry-leading API documentation and integration simplicity Payment Innovation : Pioneered features like Pay with Bank and Direct Debit in Nigerian market Reliability : Exceptional uptime and payment success rates Stripe Backing : Access to Stripe’s global infrastructure, expertise, and resources Best For : Startups and digital businesses prioritizing quick integration, developers seeking excellent documentation and support, businesses focused on Nigerian and Ghanaian markets, and tech companies valuing modern payment infrastructure. 5. DPO Group (A Network International Company) Overview : Established in 2006 initially serving Kenya’s airline and travel sectors, DPO Group systematically acquired five payment companies between 2016-2019 to build comprehensive payment infrastructure across Southern and Eastern Africa. Geographic Coverage : Operations across 21 African countries with strongest presence in Southern and Eastern Africa. Core Strengths : Largest PSP in Southern Africa : Dominant position in South African market and neighboring countries Enterprise Payment Processing : Strong track record serving airlines, hotels, and large e-commerce platforms Integrated Platform : Acquisitions created unified platform handling payment processing, mobile money, card issuing, and bank transfers 60,000+ Merchants : Extensive merchant base across travel, hospitality, and e-commerce sectors Best For : Businesses operating in Southern and Eastern Africa, travel and hospitality companies, enterprises requiring comprehensive payment processing, and businesses needing established banking partnerships in the region. 6. Cellulant (Tingg) Overview : Founded in 2003 as a mobile content company, Cellulant transformed into a payments infrastructure provider. The company’s Tingg platform provides unified access to 120 financial service providers across 34 African countries. Geographic Coverage : 34 countries across Sub-Saharan Africa, strongest in East and West Africa. Core Strengths : Single API Access : One integration connecting 120 financial service providers, 40 mobile network operators, and 600+ businesses Scale : Processed 214 million transactions totaling $12.3 billion in 2021 Mobile Money Expertise : Deep relationships with mobile network operators across the continent Omnichannel Capabilities : Cards, mobile money, bank transfers, and cross-border payments Best For : Businesses requiring maximum African geographic coverage, companies with strong mobile money collection needs, enterprises seeking single integration for continent-wide access, and logistics/delivery businesses needing diverse payment options. 7. Onafriq (Formerly MFS Africa) Overview : Launched in 2009 to solve Africa’s mobile money interoperability problem, Onafriq built API infrastructure bridging isolated mobile money networks. Strategic acquisitions of Beyonic, Baxi, and Global Technology Partners expanded capabilities into B2B payments, agent banking, and card processing. Geographic Coverage : Pan-African with particularly strong mobile money network coverage. Core Strengths : Mobile Wallet Connectivity : Nearly 1 billion mobile wallets and 500 million bank accounts in network Remittance Infrastructure : Major player in African remittance corridors Agent Network : 90,000+ agent touchpoints through Baxi acquisition Card Processing : Connects 80+ banks across 34 countries to major card networks Best For : Businesses focused on mobile money collections across multiple countries, remittance and cross-border payment needs, businesses requiring agent network access, and companies serving customers without traditional banking access. How to Choose the Right B2B Payment System for Your African Business Selecting the optimal B2B payment solution represents a critical decision affecting operations, growth potential, and customer relationships. Here’s a comprehensive framework for evaluation: 1. Define Your Geographic Requirements Current and Future Markets : Identify which African countries you operate in currently and plan to expand to within 2-3 years. Payment provider coverage varies significantly by region. Regional Specialization vs. Pan-African : Determine whether you need deep capabilities in specific countries (suggesting regional specialists) or broad coverage across many markets (suggesting pan-African providers). Cross-Border Needs : Assess the volume and importance of cross-border transactions. If substantial, prioritize providers with strong multi-country capabilities and favorable exchange rates. 2. Analyze Your Transaction Profile Transaction Volumes and Values : Calculate average transaction values, monthly volumes, and projected growth. Some providers are optimized for high-volume, lower-value transactions while others excel at larger enterprise payments. Payment Methods Required : Identify which payment methods your customers and suppliers prefer: If mobile money dominates: Prioritize providers with strong mobile money coverage If cards are important: Ensure robust card processing capabilities If bank transfers prevail: Focus on efficient bank payment infrastructure If diverse methods needed: Choose providers offering comprehensive options Payment Direction : Determine whether you primarily need to collect payments (pay-ins), send payments (payouts), or both, as provider capabilities vary. Recurring vs. One-Time : If you have subscription or recurring payment models, prioritize providers with strong recurring billing and automated payment features. 3. Evaluate Integration and Technical Requirements Technical Resources : Honestly assess your team’s technical capabilities: Strong development team : API-first providers with comprehensive documentation Limited technical resources : No-code or low-code solutions with payment links and hosted checkout pages Enterprise IT infrastructure : Providers with established ERP and accounting software integrations Time to Market : Balance speed requirements against customization needs. Payment links and hosted solutions enable faster deployment, while custom API integrations provide greater control but require more development time. Existing System Integration : Map your current technology stack (accounting software, ERP, CRM, e-commerce platform) and prioritize payment providers offering native integrations or well-documented APIs. Scalability Requirements : Ensure chosen solutions can handle 5-10x growth in transaction volume without requiring platform migration. 4. Assess Cost Structure and Total Cost of Ownership Payment pricing in Africa varies significantly across providers and payment methods. Conduct thorough cost analysis: Transaction Fees : Compare percentage fees and fixed costs across payment methods. A provider charging 2.5% on card payments but 5% on mobile money may be expensive if mobile money dominates your transactions. Hidden Costs : Identify all potential costs including: Setup and integration fees Monthly platform fees or minimums Currency conversion markups Settlement fees Chargeback and dispute fees API call fees Support and account management fees Cost at Scale : Project costs at different transaction volumes. Some providers offer volume discounts making them more competitive at scale. Payment Method Economics : Different payment methods carry different costs: Cards: Typically 2.5-4% Bank transfers: Often fixed fees or lower percentages Mobile money: Variable, typically 1-4% Virtual accounts: Usually lower cost per transaction Total Cost of Ownership : Include internal costs like development time, ongoing maintenance, reconciliation labor, and failed payment handling when calculating true cost. 5. Prioritize Security and Compliance Security and regulatory compliance are non-negotiable in B2B payment selection: Security Certifications : Require providers holding: PCI DSS compliance (for card payments) ISO 27001 (information security management) ISO 22301 (business continuity) Data Protection : Ensure providers encrypt sensitive data, implement multi-factor authentication, and follow data protection best practices. Fraud Prevention : Evaluate fraud detection capabilities including: Real-time transaction monitoring AML (Anti-Money Laundering) screening Identity verification tools Customizable fraud rules Regulatory Compliance : Confirm providers hold necessary licenses and comply with central bank regulations in your operating countries. Non-compliant providers create legal risks. Business Continuity : Assess provider uptime history, redundancy measures, and disaster recovery capabilities. Payment system downtime directly impacts revenue. 6. Evaluate Settlement Speed and Currency Options Settlement Timing : Compare settlement speeds: Instant settlement (same day) T+1 (next business day) T+2 to T+5 (2-5 business days) Faster settlement dramatically improves cash flow but may carry higher costs. Multi-Currency Capabilities : If operating across multiple countries, evaluate: Which African currencies are supported Currency conversion rates and transparency Ability to hold balances in multiple currencies Multi-currency settlement options (collect in one currency, settle in another) Currency Risk Management : Some providers offer tools to lock exchange rates or provide hedging options for businesses exposed to currency volatility. 7. Consider User Experience and Support Dashboard and Reporting : Evaluate the merchant dashboard for: Real-time transaction visibility Comprehensive reporting and analytics Export capabilities for accounting integration Payment reconciliation tools Refund and dispute management Customer Payment Experience : Test the checkout or payment flow from customer perspective: Load times and reliability Mobile responsiveness Number of steps to complete payment Available payment methods Clear error messages Support Quality : Assess provider support through: Availability : 24/7 support vs. business hours Channels : Phone, email, chat, dedicated account management Response times : SLA commitments for issue resolution Technical support : Developer support quality and documentation Local presence : Support teams understanding African market context 8. Verify Track Record and Reliability Market Reputation : Research provider reputation through: Customer reviews and testimonials Case studies from similar businesses Industry awards and recognition Media coverage and analyst reports Uptime History : Payment system downtime directly impacts revenue. Require transparency on historical uptime and service level agreements (SLAs). Financial Stability : Assess provider financial health and backing. Well-funded or profitable providers are more likely to maintain service quality and continue innovation. Client Portfolio : Review provider’s client base. If serving businesses similar to yours successfully, that indicates capability alignment. 9. Plan for Growth and Flexibility Scalability : Ensure solutions scale seamlessly as transaction volumes increase without requiring migration to new platforms. Geographic Expansion : If planning expansion to new African markets, prioritize providers already operating in target countries or with clear expansion roadmaps. Product Roadmap : Understand provider innovation plans. Are they investing in features you’ll need in the future? Lock-In Risks : Assess switching costs and data portability. Avoid solutions creating excessive vendor lock-in that limits future flexibility. 10. Conduct Thorough Due Diligence Pilot Testing : Before full commitment, run pilot programs with shortlisted providers to test integration, performance, and support quality. Reference Checks : Speak with current customers, particularly businesses similar to yours, about their experiences. Contract Review : Carefully review contracts for hidden fees, service level commitments, liability limitations, and termination clauses. Implementation Planning : Work with providers to develop detailed implementation plans including timelines, responsibilities, testing protocols, and go-live procedures. Future Trends in African B2B Payments Africa’s B2B payment landscape continues evolving rapidly. Understanding emerging trends helps businesses make forward-looking decisions and maintain competitive advantage. 1. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Integration AI and ML technologies are transforming B2B payment operations: Intelligent Reconciliation : AI-powered systems automatically match payments to invoices even with incomplete information, using pattern recognition to identify corresponding transactions. These systems learn from corrections, continuously improving accuracy. Predictive Analytics : Machine learning models analyze historical payment patterns to predict when customers will pay, helping businesses forecast cash flow more accurately and identify late payment risks early. Fraud Detection : Advanced AI monitors transaction patterns in real-time, identifying suspicious activities and blocking fraudulent payments before completion. These systems detect subtle anomalies humans miss. Smart Payment Routing : AI optimizes payment routing across multiple rails, automatically selecting the fastest, cheapest, or most reliable path based on amount, destination, time, and other factors. Chatbot Support : AI-powered chatbots handle routine payment inquiries, status checks, and troubleshooting, providing 24/7 support while freeing human agents for complex issues. 2. Blockchain and Digital Currency Exploration While still emerging, blockchain technology and digital currencies present interesting possibilities for African B2B payments: Stablecoin Settlements : Some businesses are experimenting with stablecoin-based cross-border payments, potentially offering faster settlements and lower costs than traditional correspondent banking. Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) : Several African central banks (Nigeria’s eNaira, Ghana’s eCedi exploration) are developing or piloting CBDCs that could eventually provide efficient B2B payment rails. Smart Contracts : Blockchain-based smart contracts could automate payment release based on verified delivery or milestone completion, reducing disputes and improving supply chain efficiency. Transparency and Traceability : Blockchain provides immutable transaction records valuable for audit trails, supply chain verification, and compliance documentation. Challenges : Regulatory uncertainty, volatility (even with stablecoins), limited adoption, and infrastructure requirements currently limit mainstream B2B blockchain payment adoption in Africa. 3. Real-Time Payments Expansion Real-time payment systems are expanding across Africa, transforming B2B payment expectations: Instant Settlement : More countries are implementing real-time payment infrastructure (like Nigeria’s NIBSS Instant Payment) enabling 24/7/365 instant transfers. Improved Cash Flow : Real-time payments fundamentally change working capital management, enabling businesses to operate with less capital tied up in payment float. Request to Pay : Emerging “request to pay” features allow businesses to send payment requests that customers can approve and pay instantly, streamlining collections. 24/7 Operations : Real-time systems eliminate banking hours constraints, enabling payments anytime including weekends and holidays. 4. Embedded Finance and Banking-as-a-Service B2B payment providers are increasingly offering embedded financial services: Working Capital Access : Payment platforms use transaction data to offer instant access to working capital loans, invoice financing, and credit lines without separate bank applications. Multi-Currency Wallets : Businesses can hold balances in multiple currencies within payment platforms, managing forex exposure strategically. Business Banking Services : Payment providers are expanding into full business banking, offering accounts, cards, and financial management tools alongside payment processing. Supply Chain Finance : Integrated platforms enable supplier early payment programs, buyer financing, and other supply chain financial solutions. 5. Open Banking and API Ecosystems Open banking principles are gradually emerging in African markets: Bank Account Payments : Direct bank account debits and credits without card intermediation, reducing costs while improving success rates. Account Verification : Instant verification of bank account ownership and balance information, reducing fraud and payment failures. Financial Data Sharing : With customer consent, businesses can access financial data enabling better credit decisions and personalized services. API Standardization : Gradual movement toward standardized APIs across financial institutions, reducing integration complexity. 6. Increased Automation and Integration B2B payment processes are becoming increasingly automated: ERP Integration : Deeper integration between payment systems and enterprise resource planning software, enabling automatic payment initiation based on approved invoices. Accounts Payable Automation : End-to-end AP automation from invoice receipt through approval workflows to payment execution and reconciliation. Subscription and Recurring Billing : Sophisticated recurring payment management with automatic retry logic, dunning management, and subscription lifecycle handling. API-First Architecture : Modern payment platforms prioritize API access, enabling businesses to build custom workflows and integrations matching their unique processes. 7. Enhanced Customer Experience Focus B2B payment providers increasingly prioritize user experience: Consumer-Grade Interfaces : Business payment dashboards and flows adopting consumer-app simplicity and intuitiveness. Mobile-First Design : Recognition that many African business owners manage operations primarily via smartphone, driving mobile-optimized experiences. Self-Service Capabilities : Comprehensive self-service portals reducing need for support intervention while empowering businesses with control. Personalization : Tailored experiences based on business type, transaction patterns, and preferences. 8. Regulatory Evolution and Harmonization African payment regulations continue evolving: AfCFTA Payment Integration : Continental free trade area driving initiatives to harmonize payment regulations and create cross-border payment infrastructure. Open Banking Regulations : Countries beginning to implement open banking frameworks requiring banks to share data via APIs with customer consent. Digital Currency Regulation : Central banks developing regulatory frameworks for digital currencies, stablecoins, and crypto-assets. Consumer Protection : Strengthening regulations protecting businesses and consumers in digital payments, including dispute resolution and liability frameworks. Conclusion: The Future of B2B Payments in Africa Africa’s B2B payments landscape stands at a transformative inflection point. The combination of expanding digital infrastructure, innovative payment providers, regulatory evolution, and changing business expectations is creating unprecedented opportunities for businesses willing to modernize their payment operations. The Opportunity Ahead For African businesses, optimizing B2B payments represents far more than operational efficiency—it’s a strategic enabler of growth, competitiveness, and continental expansion. Businesses that embrace modern payment infrastructure position themselves to: Scale Rapidly : Unified payment APIs enable expansion into new African markets in weeks rather than months, removing payment barriers that previously limited geographic growth. Compete Globally : Efficient payment infrastructure allows African businesses to serve international customers and suppliers with the same reliability as businesses in developed markets. Improve Profitability : Reducing payment costs by 30-60% while accelerating cash flow directly impacts bottom-line profitability and reduces financing costs. Access Financial Services : Digital payment track records unlock access to working capital, trade finance, and other financial services that drive business growth. Build Stronger Relationships : Reliable, convenient payment experiences strengthen relationships with customers and suppliers, creating competitive differentiation. The Path Forward Success in modernizing B2B payments requires: Strategic Thinking : Approach payment transformation as strategic initiative, not just operational upgrade. Align payment capabilities with business growth objectives. Appropriate Solutions : Select payment providers and methods matching your specific business requirements, transaction profile, and geographic footprint. Thoughtful Implementation : Invest adequate time in planning, testing, training, and phased rollout to ensure successful adoption. Continuous Optimization : Treat payment optimization as ongoing process, continuously refining approaches based on performance data and changing needs. Ecosystem Mindset : Recognize that payment providers are partners in your growth, not just vendors. Build collaborative relationships leveraging their expertise. A Continental Vision At the macro level, efficient B2B payment infrastructure is fundamental to realizing Africa’s economic potential. The African Continental Free Trade Area creates a $3.4 trillion market, but that potential remains theoretical without payment systems enabling frictionless cross-border trade. Every business that modernizes its B2B payments contributes to building Africa’s digital payment infrastructure. Collectively, these decisions create network effects—as more businesses adopt digital payments, the value increases for everyone. The hidden opportunities in Africa’s $200+ billion B2B payments market are becoming less hidden every day. The question is no longer whether to modernize your B2B payment operations, but how quickly you can implement changes that position your business for success in Africa’s digital economy. The transformation is underway. The infrastructure exists. The opportunity awaits. African businesses that act decisively to optimize their B2B payments will be the ones capturing market share, expanding across borders, and building the next generation of African commerce. body_text: KORU Medical Systems to Participate in the Canaccord Genuity 46th Annual Growth Conference July 29, 2026 4:05 pm EDT Download as PDF MAHWAH, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- KORU Medical Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ: KRMD) (“KORU Medical” or the “Company”), a leading medical technology company focused on development, manufacturing, and commercialization of innovative and patient-centric large volume subcutaneous infusion solutions, today announced that the Company will participate in the Canaccord Genuity 46th Annual Growth Conference on August 12th, 2026. KORU Medical's management is scheduled to present at the Canaccord Genuity 46th Annual Growth Conference on August 12th, 2026, at 10:00 am ET. Interested parties can access the live and archived webcast on the News/Events page of the Investors section of KORU Medical’s website at www.korumedical.com . About KORU Medical Systems KORU Medical develops, manufactures, and commercializes innovative and patient-centric subcutaneous infusion solutions that improve quality of life for patients around the world. The Freedom Syringe Infusion System (the “Freedom System”) currently includes the Freedom60® and FreedomEDGE® Syringe Infusion Drivers, Precision Flow Rate Tubing™ and High-Flo Subcutaneous Safety Needle Sets™. The Freedom System, which received its first FDA clearance in 1994, is used for self-administration in the home by the patient and/or delivery in an ambulatory infusion center by a healthcare professional. Through its Pharma Services and Clinical Trials business, KORU Medical provides products for use by biopharmaceutical companies in feasibility/clinical trials during the drug development process and, as needed, is capable of customizing the Freedom System for clinical and commercial use across multiple drug categories. For more information, please visit www.korumedical.com .
